name: Orca
tagline: A developer tooling product shipped under the Orca name, with a thin public footprint at the time of writing.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Honest caveat up front: this is a small, recently shipped developer tool and we have not verified its feature surface or pricing, so treat the verdict as provisional. Tools in this shape usually reduce to a thin layer over APIs you already have tokens for, which is exactly the sort of thing an agent can stand up locally in a sitting. The gaps are the boring ones: OAuth flows, webhook receivers that need a public URL, and keeping up with upstream API churn after the novelty wears off. A personal replacement will cover your own repos and your own habits and nothing else, which for one developer is often enough. Revisit this entry once the product surface is actually documented.
coreLoopDIY: A local-first dashboard and CLI that pulls your repos, pull requests, CI runs and recent commits into one SQLite-backed view you can refresh on demand.
requirements: A GitHub personal access token with repo and workflow read scopes
Somewhere to leave a process running if you want scheduled refreshes
whatYouLose: Hosted dashboards your teammates can open without cloning your repo
Real-time webhooks instead of polling, which means no public URL to maintain
Integrations beyond whatever two APIs you bothered to wire up
Someone else absorbing upstream API changes and rate limit surprises
Any mobile or notification story worth the name
moatNotes: Nothing structural visible yet. For young dev tools the moat is usually taste and the breadth of integrations, both of which take time rather than cleverness.
whyPeopleStillPay: Developers pay for tooling that removes a daily irritation without becoming a side project. A self-built dashboard is fun on Saturday and abandoned by the third API deprecation, and the hosted version keeps working while you are busy doing the actual job. If the product turns out to sit on a team workflow rather than a solo one, the shared-state argument gets considerably stronger and the DIY build gets considerably weaker.
notes: Provisional entry: the product is early and we are judging the category more than the app. Worth a recheck once there is real documentation to read.
prompt:
Build a local-first developer workflow dashboard. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- TypeScript everywhere, Node 20+
- Next.js (App Router) for the UI, run with `npm run dev`
- SQLite via better-sqlite3 as the only datastore, file at ./data/orca.db
- Tailwind for styling, no component library
- A single CLI entry point via tsx: `npm run sync`

What it does:
1. Reads GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_LOGIN from .env (provide .env.example, never commit secrets).
2. `npm run sync` calls the GitHub REST API and upserts into SQLite: repos you own or contribute to, open pull requests assigned to or opened by you, the latest workflow run per repo with its conclusion, and the 20 most recent commits per active repo.
3. Handles pagination, respects rate limit headers, and backs off on 403 with a clear log line.
4. The dashboard has exactly three pages: Overview (open PRs grouped by repo, red badge for failing CI), Repos (table sorted by last push, with CI status and open PR count), and Activity (reverse chronological commit feed).
5. A Sync button in the header triggers the same sync via a POST route and shows the last sync timestamp read from the database.

Explicitly out of scope: OAuth, webhooks, multi-user support, notifications, GitLab or Bitbucket, deploys, writing anything back to GitHub, Docker, hosting.

Deliverables: working code, a schema.sql, a README with setup in under ten lines, and seed-free first run that fails loudly if the token is missing.
Keep the whole thing under roughly 800 lines. Favour boring, readable code over abstraction.
